tagline: Pronounced curves and stone masonry carry a highway across the Smokies.
intro: Newfound Gap Road climbs through pronounced curves to overlooks within Great Smoky Mountains National Park. The 31-mile connection between Gatlinburg, Tennessee, and Cherokee, North Carolina, is an All-American Road. The Federal Highway Administration highlights its river access, vegetation and stone masonry, describing a landscape shaped by the National Park Service’s rustic design. Tennessee’s transportation department identifies scenic and historic qualities here, including bridges, tunnels and walls retained from the 1930s and early 1940s.

An earlier crossing used Indian Gap Road, an arduous, unpaved route completed in 1839. In 1872, Arnold Guyot’s measurements established Newfound Gap as a lower, more accessible pass. As the national park developed, a new Tennessee-to-North Carolina highway crossed this gap; completed in 1932, it replaced Indian Gap Road. The road was designed both to link the states and to give motorists and hikers carefully planned views of the landscape.

From Gatlinburg, the drive runs toward Newfound Gap and the North Carolina side of the park. The Chimney Tops trailhead is along Newfound Gap Road, about 6.9 miles southeast of Sugarlands Visitor Center. At the gap, US 441 meets the state line and the Appalachian Trail. Kuwohi Road branches off just past Newfound Gap toward the observation tower; the through route continues to Cherokee.

moments.title: Chimney Tops
moments.text: Two bare rock points give Chimney Tops its distinctive summit. It is one of the Smokies’ few bare rock summits, with bedrock chiefly composed of slate, phyllite and metasiltstone. The 2016 fire changed the approach: the trail reopened in October 2017 with a new observation area overlooking both points. The fire’s extreme heat accelerated weathering of the exposed rock and raised concerns over rock movement, prompting a prohibition on summit access. At the mountain’s base, the Road Prong Trail follows an older route known in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries as the Indian Gap Trail.

moments.title: Newfound Gap
moments.text: At 5,048 feet, Newfound Gap brings a highway, a state boundary and the Appalachian Trail together. The Tennessee–North Carolina line crosses the pass, as does US 441. The Rockefeller Memorial marks another meeting here: President Franklin D. Roosevelt formally dedicated the national park at this site on September 2, 1940. Beyond the road crossing, the Appalachian Trail and other paths wind through the area’s spruce-fir forest. The highway had been completed eight years before the dedication. The roadside overlooks here occupy the highway’s highest elevation, with the memorial beside this crossing between the two states.

moments.title: Kuwohi
moments.text: A spiral ramp leads to Kuwohi’s circular observation platform, a concrete structure built in 1959. The tower belonged to Mission 66, the National Park Service program that expanded facilities for the influx of visitors after World War II. Architect Hubert Bebb’s concrete design departed from the rustic materials favored in earlier park buildings. It stands on Tennessee’s highest mountain, at 6,643 feet, reached from the parking area by a steep, half-mile paved trail. Spruce-fir forest covers the mountain, a forest type confined in the southeastern United States to its highest elevations.
moments.notice: Look for the circular platform and spiral ramp of the 1959 observation tower.
